title: Study Points to Europe as the Birthplace of Bats
summary:
For decades, scientists have debated where bats first appeared. Africa, Asia, and North America were all proposed as possible birthplaces. New research now points to Europe.

An international team of 137 researchers from 64 countries combined genomic data from every living bat family with evidence from ancient fossils. The work was carried out through the Bat1K consortium, a global effort to sequence the genomes of all living bat species, co-founded by Professor Emma Teeling of University College Dublin. The study was published in Nature.

The researchers examined 103 bat genomes, including 42 newly generated chromosome-level assemblies, covering all 21 recognized bat families. They also incorporated evidence from 44 fossil bats. Together, these data gave a much clearer picture of how bats emerged and spread.

The results suggest bats first evolved in Europe during the late Paleocene, roughly 65 to 60 million years ago. Their descendants then moved into Africa. As bats diversified, separate groups expanded into the Americas, Asia, and Australia, producing the major lineages found today.

Bats are among the most distinctive mammals. They are the only mammals capable of sustained powered flight, and most species navigate and hunt in darkness using echolocation, or sound. They represent about one fifth of all living mammals and play important ecological roles. Many bat species are unusually resistant to disease and live far longer than other mammals of similar size.

"It is extraordinary, after decades of research and conflicting findings, we finally have a robust phylogenetic tree that we can now use to properly understand how and where bats' unique traits evolved," said Teeling, co-founding director of Bat1K. She added that the genomes can help uncover the molecular basis of these adaptations.

The findings also offer clues about powered flight and echolocation. "As bats are the only mammals known to have evolved true powered flight, our findings point to Europe as the most likely place where mammalian powered flight first evolved," Teeling said.

Researchers also analyzed the fossil bat Vielasia, which sits on the oldest branch of the bat family tree. That fossil suggests echolocation had already appeared close to the beginning of bat evolution. Taken together, the evidence indicates both powered flight and echolocation emerged before modern bat groups began diversifying, possibly helping drive the group's success.

"The approach we used to model the evolution of fossil and living species together can do what other methods cannot," said senior author Professor Liliana M. Dávalos of Stony Brook University.
why_it_matters: Bats are the only mammals capable of powered flight, so understanding their origins helps scientists learn how remarkable traits like flight and echolocation evolved.
